cards.title: What Is an Entity?
cards.teaser: An entity is a domain object defined by identity that persists across state changes. The object's data can change entirely — its name, address, status, balance — and it remains the same thing, because sameness is determined by who it is, not what it contains.

runs.text: Eric Evans introduced the term
Entity
in
Domain-Driven Design
(2003) to describe domain objects whose thread of identity runs through time and transformation. An entity has two defining properties:

items.text: that distinguishes it from all other objects of the same type, regardless of attribute values.
— its attributes can change over its lifetime without affecting its identity.

runs.text: A
Customer

is an entity. The customer moves, marries, changes their email address, upgrades their subscription, and accumulates 10 years of order history. Throughout all of this, they are the same customer — identified by customer ID
, not by name or address.
This contrasts sharply with
Value Objects
, which have no identity — they are defined entirely by their attribute values. Two
Money(100, USD)
instances are interchangeable. Two
Customer(id=C-44821)
instances represent the same real-world person even if one has stale data.

Evans's definition: "An object defined primarily by its identity is called an Entity." The key word is "primarily" — the identity is the load-bearing part of the definition, not the current snapshot of attributes.

An entity is a thing in your domain that keeps being itself even as its details change. A person is still the same person after they move, marry, or change jobs. That continuous sameness — tracked by an ID — is what makes it an entity.

cards.title: The Classic Test: Same Thing If Data Changes?
cards.teaser: The fastest way to decide whether something is an entity or a value object is a single question: if every attribute of this object changed, would it still make sense to call it the same thing? If yes, it is an entity. If no — if changing all its attributes makes it a new thing — it is a value object.

runs.text: The classic test comes from Evans's observation that entities maintain continuity of identity through state change. Apply it by imagining complete attribute replacement:

items.text: whose balance changes from $1,000 to $500 is still the same account — same account number, same history.
amount whose value changes from $1,000 to $500 is a different amount — there is no continuity of identity to preserve.
whose status changes from PENDING to SHIPPED is still the same order — the customer, the business, and the warehouse all care about the history of that specific order.
with different street and city values is simply a different address.

runs.text: The edge case that trips people up: objects that appear stateful but are actually values. A
DateRange
has two attributes and can be "modified" by creating a new one. It does not need tracking across time.
Value Object.
Conversely, a
Seat
in a concert venue looks like a simple value (row A, seat 14) but needs to be reserved, transferred, and marked as occupied — it has a lifecycle.
Entity.
A related test: does the domain care about the history of this object? If auditors, customers, or the system itself need to know "what happened to this specific thing over time," it is an entity.

Ask: if all the data changed, would this still be the same thing? Your bank account is still your account even if the balance hits zero. A $100 bill replaced by a $50 bill is not the same bill — it is a different value. The first is an entity; the second is a value object.

cards.title: Entity vs Value Object: The Decision
cards.teaser: Choosing entity vs value object is one of the most consequential modeling decisions in DDD. The choice determines identity semantics, equality logic, mutability, persistence strategy, and lifecycle management. Getting it wrong creates objects that are hard to reason about, hard to test, and hard to persist.

runs.text: The decision is driven by how the domain thinks about the object, not by how the database stores it or how the code happens to be structured. Ask three questions:

items.text: Does the domain care about tracking this specific instance over time?
If yes — entity. Tracking implies identity, history, and lifecycle.
Are two instances with the same attributes interchangeable?
If yes — value object. Interchangeability means there is no meaningful distinction between instances.
Does the object have a lifecycle with distinct states (active, suspended, archived)?
If yes — entity. State machines imply persistence of something across transitions.

runs.text: Consequences of the wrong choice:

items.text: Treating a value object as an entity
— creates spurious IDs, adds join tables or foreign keys, and forces mutable state onto objects that should be immutable. Example: giving
an ID and tracking it in a database row.
Treating an entity as a value object
— loses history, breaks referential integrity, and makes it impossible to correlate events with the same real-world thing. Example: replacing an
record instead of updating it, severing their performance review and leave history.

runs.text: Default to value object when in doubt. Entities carry more cost (ID management, lifecycle, equality logic). Use entities only when the domain genuinely requires tracking a specific instance over time.

If the domain needs to say 'this is the same thing as before' after a change, use an entity. If two instances with equal attributes are totally interchangeable, use a value object. When unsure, start with a value object — it is cheaper to upgrade than to downgrade.

cards.title: Identity Allocation: DB-Generated IDs
cards.teaser: Database-generated IDs (auto-increment integers, sequences) are the simplest identity strategy — the database assigns the ID on INSERT. The cost is that the object has no identity until it is persisted, which breaks the domain model's ability to work with entities before they touch a database.

runs.text: The pattern is ubiquitous: declare a column as
SERIAL
or
BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT
, and the database fills in the ID when the row is inserted. The application receives the generated key via
RETURNING id
or
LAST_INSERT_ID()
Advantages:

items.text: Compact integer IDs that are human-readable and storage-efficient.
Natural sort order matches insertion order — useful for pagination.

runs.text: Costs:

items.text: The entity cannot reference itself, cannot be placed in an in-memory set or map, and cannot be correlated with other objects until it has been saved. This violates the DDD principle that domain objects should be fully functional independent of persistence.
Creating an entity means going to the database before you can do further work with it. In unit tests this forces awkward mocking. In distributed systems it creates a synchronous bottleneck.

Integer IDs are not globally unique. Merging datasets from two databases that both use auto-increment IDs creates conflicts. This is a real problem in multi-tenancy, data imports, and microservice architectures.
Sequential integers expose object count and make it trivially easy to enumerate all records by incrementing an ID in a URL.

runs.text: The "no identity before INSERT" problem is the deepest DDD concern. If your entity factory creates a transient object with id=None, then domain events referencing that object, equality checks, and aggregate membership tests are all broken until the database responds.

DB-generated IDs are simple and reliable but they make the database the source of identity. Until a record is saved, the entity does not exist as far as the domain is concerned — which is backwards from how good domain models should work.

cards.title: Identity Allocation: Application-Generated UUID
cards.teaser: Application-generated UUIDs assign identity before the entity touches a database. The application creates the ID — typically a UUID v4 — at object construction time, making the entity fully functional from birth. This removes the wait-for-INSERT bottleneck and enables distributed, pre-commit identity.

runs.text: A UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is a 128-bit value, typically formatted as
. UUID v4 is randomly generated with 122 bits of entropy, giving a collision probability of roughly 1 in 10^18 for a billion IDs. For practical purposes, collision is impossible.
With application-generated UUIDs, the entity factory looks like this:

explanation.code:
import uuid

class Order:
    def __init__(self, customer_id: str, items: list):
        self.id = str(uuid.uuid4())   # identity assigned at construction
        self.customer_id = customer_id
        self.items = items
        self.status = "PENDING"

# The order has a stable identity immediately:
order = Order(customer_id="C-44821", items=[...])
print(order.id)  # 7f3c9e2a-4b1d-4a6f-8d2e-9c3a1b5f7e2d
# Can now add to sets, maps, reference in events — before any INSERT

runs.text: Advantages:

items.text: Domain events, aggregate membership, and in-memory references all work before persistence.
No collision across databases, services, or merged datasets.
Multiple application nodes can generate IDs simultaneously without coordination.
Random UUIDs reveal nothing about total record count or insertion order.

runs.text: Costs:

items.text: 16 bytes vs 4-8 bytes for an integer. Meaningful in high-volume tables with many foreign key references.
Random insertion order hurts B-tree indexes.
UUID v4 inserts scatter across the index, causing page splits and cache misses at scale. This is the key motivation for ordered UUID alternatives.
Debugging and log tracing is harder with 36-character strings than with integer IDs.

runs.text: Application-generated UUIDs give entities a full identity the moment they are created in memory — no database round trip needed. The tradeoff is that random UUIDs are bad for database indexes at high volume, which is the problem ULID was invented to solve.

cards.title: ULID and KSUID: Sortable UUID Alternatives
cards.teaser: ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) and KSUID (K-Sortable Unique ID) solve the UUID v4 index-scatter problem by embedding a time prefix into the ID. The result: globally unique, application-generated, pre-INSERT identity that is also roughly sorted by creation time.

runs.text: Both formats interleave timestamp bits with random bits so that IDs generated close in time sort close together in a B-tree index — dramatically reducing page splits.
ULID structure:

items.text: — encodes time to the millisecond, valid until year 10889.

runs.text: KSUID (Segment) structure:

items.text: — coarser than ULID, but still sorts records by second of creation.
— more random bits than ULID, lower collision probability.

runs.text: Comparison table:

UUID v7 (RFC 9562, 2024) standardizes the time-prefixed UUID approach at the IETF level, using a 48-bit Unix timestamp prefix with 74 random bits. UUID v7 is the emerging standard that may eventually supersede ULID in new systems.

ULID and KSUID are UUIDs that start with a timestamp. That timestamp makes them sort chronologically — new records end up next to other recent records in the database index, which keeps the index compact and cache-friendly. Same pre-INSERT benefits as UUID v4, but with better database performance.

cards.title: Natural Keys vs Surrogate Keys
cards.teaser: A natural key is an identifier from the domain itself — a passport number, an ISBN, a stock ticker symbol. A surrogate key is a system-generated identifier with no domain meaning. Both can serve as entity identity; the choice has consequences for stability, privacy, and cross-system integration.

runs.text: Natural keys are appealing because they exist in the domain without the system having to create them. Some examples where natural keys are reliable:

items.text: for books — assigned by publishers, globally unique, stable for the life of the edition.
(International Securities Identification Number) for financial instruments — standardized, globally recognized.
— globally unique at a point in time, but
— people change email addresses, which is why this is usually a bad natural key.

runs.text: The danger with natural keys is that the domain's guarantees are often weaker than they appear:

items.text: — the Social Security Administration reuses numbers after a period.
— a number reassigned to a new user breaks any system that treated it as a stable identifier.

runs.text: The standard DDD recommendation: use a
surrogate key
(UUID, ULID, or auto-increment) as the technical identity, and store the natural key as a
domain attribute

with a unique constraint. The entity's identity is stable even if the natural key changes (e.g., a user changes their email). Queries can still use the natural key; the surrogate key handles the identity contract.
If a natural key changes in real life, every foreign key that referenced it breaks. Surrogate keys decouple the system's identity contract from the domain's volatile data.

A natural key comes from the real world (like a passport number); a surrogate key is invented by the system (like a UUID). Natural keys are tempting but tend to change or repeat unexpectedly. The safe approach: use a surrogate key as the true ID and store the natural key as just another attribute.

cards.title: Identity Equality: equals() Uses ID, Not State
cards.teaser: For entities, equality means same identity — two entity instances are equal if and only if they have the same ID. Comparing attributes is explicitly wrong, because the same entity can exist in two different in-memory states (a cached version and a freshly loaded version) and must still compare as equal.

runs.text: This is one of the sharpest differences between entity and value object equality semantics. Value object equality is structural — compare all fields. Entity equality is identity-based — compare only the ID.
Why this matters in practice:

items.text: If equality is state-based, the same entity loaded twice appears as two distinct set members. The set grows without bound.
ORMs and repositories need to know whether an in-memory entity corresponds to an existing database row. Only identity-based equality enables correct upsert logic.
An aggregate that holds a collection of child entities must be able to determine whether a candidate entity is already in the collection. Without identity equality, duplicate entries accumulate.

runs.text: Transient entities (not yet persisted, id=None) require special care. The safest pattern: always assign an ID at construction time (application-generated UUID or ULID), ensuring no entity is ever "identity-less" even in its transient state.

Two entity objects are equal if they have the same ID — full stop. It does not matter if one has a stale email address and the other has a fresh one. They are the same customer. Comparing attribute values for entity equality is always wrong.

cards.title: Identity Scope: Global, Aggregate-Scoped, and Context-Scoped
cards.teaser: Not all entity IDs need to be globally unique. The right scope for an identity depends on where the entity lives. IDs scoped too broadly create unnecessary coordination overhead; IDs scoped too narrowly create collisions when objects cross boundaries.

runs.text: Evans identifies three practical scopes for entity identity:

items.text: — the ID must be unique across the entire system, across all contexts and services. Required for entities that are referenced by multiple bounded contexts or exposed via API. Use UUIDs, ULIDs, or database-scoped sequences with service prefixes. Example: a
entity that is referenced by the billing context, the support context, and the notifications context.
— the ID is unique only within the owning aggregate. A
can use a simple integer sequence (1, 2, 3) or a position. It is never referenced outside the
aggregate, so global uniqueness is unnecessary. Full ID is order_id + line_number.
— the ID is unique within one bounded context. A
in the support context may use a sequential integer that is meaningful and human-readable within that context (e.g., TICKET-4821) without needing global uniqueness.

runs.text: The mistake to avoid: defaulting every entity to global UUID identity. Aggregate-internal entities that get globally unique UUIDs create false flexibility — they invite other parts of the system to hold direct references to entities that should only be reachable through their aggregate root.

The DDD aggregate rule is: outside the aggregate boundary, reference the root by ID, not child entities directly. Giving child entities global IDs is a design smell that often indicates an aggregate boundary is drawn incorrectly.

Not every ID needs to be unique across the whole system. A line item inside an order only needs an ID that is unique inside that order. A customer ID needs to be globally unique because multiple systems talk about the same customer. Match the scope of the ID to the scope of the entity's visibility.

cards.title: Mutable State with Stable Identity
cards.teaser: The core property of an entity is the combination of stable identity and mutable state. The identity never changes; the state changes continuously over the entity's lifecycle. This duality — immutable thread of who, mutable thread of what — is what makes entities the natural representation of real-world objects with histories.

runs.text: Consider the lifecycle of a
Subscription
entity:
Notice the invariant:
self.id
is set in
__init__
and never touched again. Every other attribute is subject to change via explicit methods that enforce business rules. The identity anchors the history.
This is also why entity identity should be
read-only after construction
. An entity whose ID can be reassigned has no stable identity contract. In Python, enforce this with
@property
with no setter. In Java, mark the ID field
final
. In Swift, use
let

An entity is like a person: the name, address, and job can all change, but the person is still the same person (same ID). The ID is the one thing that must never change. Everything else is just the current state of that identity.

cards.title: Entity Behavior: Methods That Enforce Invariants
cards.teaser: Entities are not passive data holders — they are responsible for protecting the consistency of their own state. Every state transition goes through a method that validates preconditions and enforces business rules. An entity that allows arbitrary attribute mutation is not fulfilling its DDD role.

runs.text: The distinction between a well-designed entity and a database row with methods is
behavioral encapsulation
: the entity controls what state transitions are permitted and under what conditions.
Each method is a named domain operation —
issue
mark_paid
void
— not a generic setter. The name comes from the Ubiquitous Language. The implementation enforces the business rule. Calling code simply invokes the operation; the entity guarantees the invariant.

Evans: "An entity is responsible for the behavior rules that govern the identity through state changes." If the entity does not enforce the rules, some other object must — and that other object is now coupled to the entity's internals in a fragile way.

A well-designed entity acts like a bouncer for its own state. You do not get to set the status field directly; you call issue() or mark_paid(), and the entity decides whether the transition is valid. The entity is the authority on its own business rules.

cards.title: Anemic Entities: The Anti-Pattern
cards.teaser: An anemic entity is an entity that has been stripped of behavior — a bag of public getters and setters with no domain logic. The domain rules that should live in the entity instead end up scattered across service classes, creating fragile, duplicated, hard-to-test logic that violates the DDD model.

runs.text: Martin Fowler coined the term
Anemic Domain Model

in 2003 to describe this failure mode. It is the most common DDD anti-pattern, and it is usually the result of developers who understand the data model but treat the domain layer as a data transport layer.
The tell-tale signs of an anemic entity:

items.text: All methods are getters and setters.
with no validation. Any caller can write any value.
Business logic lives in service classes.
validates the payment and mutates the invoice directly. The logic is duplicated in
Invariants are not enforced at the point of change.
Validation happens in the service, not the entity. When a new service is added, the developer must remember to copy the validation logic — and frequently does not.
The entity is a 1:1 mirror of the database schema.
Every column becomes a field, every nullable column becomes an optional, and the model offers no semantic value beyond "I have the same shape as the table."

runs.text: Fowler's verdict: "The fundamental horror of this anti-pattern is that it's so contrary to the basic idea of object-oriented design; which is to combine data and process together."

If you can delete your entity classes and replace them with plain dictionaries without any test failures in the domain layer, your domain model is anemic. The behavior is somewhere else, and it is not in a good place.

An anemic entity is just a struct with a fancy name — it has fields but no rules. The rules that should belong to it get scattered across service classes. The problem is not that the entity is thin; the problem is that the rules are now duplicated, fragile, and easy to forget when adding a new service.

cards.title: Identity-Spanning-Aggregates Rule
cards.teaser: An entity belongs to exactly one aggregate at a time. When other aggregates need to reference it, they do so through the entity's ID — not through a direct object reference. This rule enforces aggregate boundaries, prevents cross-aggregate invariant entanglement, and enables safe distribution.

runs.text: Evans's rule is precise: outside an aggregate boundary, other aggregates may only hold
references by ID
to entities in other aggregates. Direct object references across aggregate roots are forbidden.
Why this matters:

items.text: holds a direct reference to a
Each aggregate is loaded, modified, and persisted in its own transaction. Direct object references invite loading two aggregates in one transaction — a consistency anti-pattern.
Aggregates can be stored in different databases or services. ID references work across service boundaries; object references do not.

explanation.code:
# WRONG: Order holds a direct Customer reference
class Order:  # anti-pattern
    def __init__(self, id: str, customer: Customer, ...):
        self.id = id
        self.customer = customer  # object reference crosses aggregate boundary


# CORRECT: Order holds only the customer's ID
class Order:  # correct DDD approach
    def __init__(self, id: str, customer_id: str, ...):
        self.id = id
        self.customer_id = customer_id  # ID reference only
        # To get customer details, query the Customer repository separately

runs.text: The practical consequence: if your domain service needs data from both aggregates, it loads them independently via their respective repositories. The service coordinates, but the aggregates remain isolated.

The rule does not prevent you from displaying a customer's name on an order screen. It prevents the Order aggregate from making decisions based on live Customer state. The order screen fetches what it needs for display; the Order aggregate enforces its own invariants with the data it owns.

An entity belongs to one aggregate. Other aggregates that need to mention it use its ID — like a foreign key — not a pointer to the actual object. This keeps each aggregate responsible for its own rules without being entangled in another aggregate's internals.

cards.title: Entity Reconstitution vs Construction
cards.teaser: Creating a new entity for the first time is not the same as loading an existing one from the database. Reconstitution bypasses creation-time business rules (like "a new account must have an opening balance > 0") because those rules were already enforced when the entity was first created.

runs.text: Conflating construction and reconstitution leads to subtle bugs. Consider a
BankAccount

that enforces a minimum opening balance of $10 in its constructor. When loading an existing account with a $0 balance from the database (the customer withdrew everything), the constructor's validation fires incorrectly and raises an error.
The standard solution is two separate creation paths:

items.text: — enforces creation invariants, generates a new ID, records a domain event.
— used by the repository — restores state from persisted data without running creation-time validations. The data is trusted: it was valid when it was saved.

runs.text: Some teams implement reconstitution via a separate static method (e.g., BankAccount.reconstitute(...)) to make the intent explicit. Others use a private constructor with a flag. The key is that the two paths exist and serve different purposes.

Creating a new entity and loading an old one from storage are different operations. When you create one, enforce all the rules for a valid new entity. When you load one, trust that the data was valid when it was saved — don't re-run creation rules that no longer apply.

cards.title: Entity Lifecycle and Domain Events
cards.teaser: Each significant state transition in an entity's lifecycle is a domain event. Capturing these events — AccountOpened, OrderShipped, SubscriptionCancelled — makes the entity's history queryable, enables event-driven integration, and decouples downstream reactions from the entity's internal logic.

runs.text: Domain events and entity lifecycle are deeply intertwined. An entity that enforces invariants through behavior methods (card 11) can record a corresponding domain event for each transition:
The
pull_events

pattern (sometimes called "outbox collection") is important: the entity collects events internally during a unit of work. The application layer saves the entity, then dispatches the events. This ensures events are only published if the save succeeds — no phantom events from failed transactions.

Domain events are the record of an entity's lifecycle. In event-sourced systems, the entity is rebuilt entirely by replaying its events. In traditional systems, events drive integration. In both cases, the entity is the source of the event — not a service observing the entity from outside.

Every meaningful thing that happens to an entity — it was created, it changed state, it was cancelled — should produce a domain event. The entity records the event internally. After the entity is saved, those events get dispatched so other parts of the system can react. The entity is the narrator of its own story.
